title: Technical Note: Using Benchmark Ensembles to Reduce the Impact of Streamflow Variability on Model Performance Metrics
content:
Abstract

Hydrologic model performance is commonly quantified with aggregated performance metrics such as the Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE). The NSE is a skill score that compares hydrologic model performance (the sum of squared errors of model residuals) to the performance obtained from using the long-term mean flow as a benchmark model (the total sum of squares). The mean flow benchmark sets different standards for model performance in different regions, which complicates model evaluation and comparison. In this study, we generalize the NSE by considering multiple benchmarks, with scores termed benchmark efficiencies (BME). We analyze spatial patterns of skill score values calculated across North America to recommend a more comprehensive method for model evaluation. Spatial patterns of BME exist for individual benchmarks due to flow variability, but selecting the lowest BME score of the ensemble at each catchment reduces bias toward individual flow regimes by comparing the model to the benchmark which best captured the unique flow variability of the catchment. The largest differences between NSE and BME occurred in strongly seasonal catchments with some catchments showing NSE values above 0.5 and negative BME values, indicating that model simulations referred to as “satisfactory” in some studies in fact failed to beat simple benchmarks. Our results demonstrate that quantifying model performance using the lowest BME score in the ensemble allows for model error to be analyzed more independently of flow variability than with the NSE, thus improving comparisons of model performance across catchments.
